analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: Previewing the Midterm Elections
key_insights: Goldman reads national sentiment as swinging 10-11pp toward Democrats since 2024, based on generic ballot polling, district-level polls, enthusiasm measures and primary turnout. Prediction markets imply a more than 90% chance Democrats win the House, on track to net 21 seats for 236 in total.

Democrats need to gain only 3 House seats. Republicans hold nearly 30 seats in districts Trump won by less than 11pp. A 236-seat majority would match the size of the 2018 majority and be wider than the roughly 220-seat majorities held since 2021.

The Senate is much closer. Prediction markets imply an over 65% chance of a Democratic majority, but Democratic leads in six Republican-held seats are within the margin of error. Only North Carolina shows a large Democratic lead.

Senate polling history argues for caution on the Democratic Senate odds. Candidates leading by 2.5pp or less in competitive races since 2002 won only 60% of the time. Republicans have beaten final polls by an average of 3pp in Republican-leaning states, and Democrats need some combination of Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa or Kansas.

The Senate result matters less for policy if Democrats win the House. Most legislation needs 60 Senate votes and Trump can veto anything Congress sends him. A Democratic Senate could block nominees, and Goldman expects Trump to push personnel changes through the current Senate before year-end if Democrats win it.

Fiscal deadlines are the main channel for legislative action. Spending authority expires Dec. 11 and Goldman expects Congress to push it to February or March 2027 rather than reach a full-year deal. The debt limit is likely reached by Q1 2027 and Congress will likely need to raise it no later than October 2027.

Fiscal policy changes are expected to be small. The fiscal impulse in 2027 is roughly neutral after the boost from last year's package. Reversing last year's spending cuts would add about 0.25% of GDP in 2027, and reinstating ACA subsidies would add about $50bn a year.

Democrats would try to roll back tariffs selectively, most likely on Canada. Goldman expects Trump to announce new tariff increases after the election, including Section 301 findings on industrial overcapacity, that more than offset the cuts. The result is a rise in the US effective tariff rate of a little under 2pp.

Goldman expects the political focus on data centers to fade after Election Day because voters rank it low among priorities. A national moratorium is unlikely, but Democrats may propose removing data centers from bonus depreciation, R&D credits and other tax incentives.

State-level data center restrictions are more likely than federal ones. Democratic gubernatorial wins could bring moratoria in places like Texas, Florida, Georgia and Michigan. Democratic trifectas in Arizona, Pennsylvania and Nevada could produce new AI-focused laws.

Federal AI regulation is possible only as a bipartisan compromise built on company-run testing and self-regulation, such as the reported Thune-Cruz-Klobuchar bill. Mandatory audits, pre-clearance of models and an AI wealth fund are unlikely to pass. If Democrats win either chamber, Goldman expects them to launch investigations into large technology companies.

The Ratepayer Protection Act, which requires states to consider data centers' effect on retail electricity consumers, will likely become law soon, possibly in a lame-duck session. Goldman expects limited impact because states keep flexibility.

sector_views.rationale: Goldman expects no sweeping federal AI or data center regulation, since Republicans block stricter rules and the White House favors an industry-led approach. Risks are tax incentive limits, congressional investigations and tighter state-level rules.

macro_indicators.reading: Rise of a little under 2pp after the election, bringing the rate to a few percentage points below its peak last year
macro_indicators.interpretation: Goldman expects new Section 301 tariffs to restore rates close to pre-Supreme Court ruling levels and more than offset any Democratic rollback.
The boost from last year's fiscal package fades, and divided government typically means less expansionary policy, though spending could rise slightly under Democratic control.

macro_indicators.indicator: Spending from reversing last year's cuts
macro_indicators.interpretation: A possible Democratic condition for extending spending authority or raising the debt limit. A discretionary or health subsidy deal would add modestly to this.

macro_indicators.reading: Likely reached by Q1 2027, with borrowing capacity constrained Aug. to Oct. 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: Treasury is expected to manage through a drawdown of its Fed balance and extraordinary measures, so Congress must act by October 2027 at the latest.

risk_factors: Senate polling errors in Republican-leaning states have favored Republicans, so Democratic leads in those races may be overstated.
A shutdown risk from the Dec. 11 expiry of spending authority and a lapse in borrowing capacity from a debt limit standoff.
Policy disputes and the distance between the two parties' spending proposals make a full-year spending deal in the lame-duck session unlikely.
Trump tariff increases after the election could more than offset Democratic rollbacks.
Thin House margins and pushback from fiscal conservatives make a Republican attempt to raise the debt limit before year-end unlikely to succeed.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: prediction market implied odds of Congressional balance of power, with more than 90% for a Democratic House and more than 65% for a Democratic Senate.
Exhibit 5: Senate midterm polling misses against state partisan lean, with Democrats outperforming polls in blue states and Republicans in red states.
Exhibit 6: Treasury borrowing capacity under the debt limit, which likely constrains borrowing from August to October 2027.
Exhibit 9: US effective tariff rate forecast, with a rise after the election from re-implementation of reciprocal rates under Section 301.
geopolitical: War in Iran: House Democrats led by Jeffries are expected to hold votes opposing it, and it is expected to be near the top of the Democratic agenda around fiscal deadlines.
US-China competition in AI is cited by Republicans and the Trump administration as a reason to oppose strict AI and data center regulation.
Tariff rollbacks would most likely focus on Canada, while the Section 301 overcapacity investigation could bring new tariffs on other partners.

tension_points.bull_case: Prediction markets give Democrats an over 65% chance of a Senate majority, and Democratic candidates lead polls in six Republican-held seats and in all the seats they are defending.
tension_points.bear_case: Most of those leads are within the margin of error. Candidates leading by 2.5pp or less won only 60% of the time since 2002, and Republicans have beaten final polls by an average of 3pp in Republican-leaning states. A Democratic lead exceeds that gap only in North Carolina.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Democrats failing to win any combination of Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa or Kansas, the states Trump won by 11-16pp that they need for 51 seats.

theme_stances.key_argument: Polling, enthusiasm and primary turnout all point to a 10-11pp swing toward Democrats, which with prediction markets implies a majority of about 236 seats.
theme_stances.evidence: Democrats Look Likely to Win the House Majority

theme_stances.key_argument: Polling in decisive Senate races is within the margin of error and past polling errors favored Republicans in red states, so market odds may overstate Democrats' position.
theme_stances.evidence: The Senate looks much closer than the House.

theme_stances.key_argument: Democratic rollbacks would be limited to a few countries or products, while new Section 301 tariffs after the election would more than offset them.
theme_stances.evidence: expect President Trump to announce new tariff increases after the election
